{
  "research_question": "How does mouse navigation performance vary across five stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) when measured by Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The dataset contains 76,655 trials across 8 mice after filtering for the five stimulation paradigms of interest.",
    "Combined stimulation accounts for the majority of trials (48,846, 63.7%), followed by ICMS Only (11,378, 14.8%), Dim Visual Only (9,603, 12.5%), Sham (3,505, 4.6%), and Bright Visual Only (3,323, 4.3%).",
    "Overall success rate across all paradigms is 72.95% (SD=0.44), with mean Time-to-Target of 2.81 seconds (SD=2.08).",
    "Path Efficiency averages 0.47 (SD=0.47) with a highly right-skewed distribution (max=29.82), suggesting some trials with very inefficient paths.",
    "Average Speed across all trials is 12.50 cm/s (SD=4.46), ranging from 0.12 to 75.35 cm/s.",
    "Angular Dispersion (AD) has mean 0.38 (SD=0.24), bounded between 0 and 1, indicating moderate directional variability in trajectories."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "Sample size imbalance is extreme: Combined has 14.7× more trials than Bright Visual Only and 13.9× more than Sham, limiting statistical power for between-paradigm comparisons.",
    "The large standard deviations relative to means for Path Efficiency (SD/mean ≈ 0.98) and Time-to-Target (SD/mean ≈ 0.74) indicate substantial within-paradigm variability that may obscure between-group effects.",
    "Success rate shows moderate variability (SD=0.44 on 0-1 scale), but without paradigm-level breakdowns, direction of effects cannot be determined from available data.",
    "The range of Average Speed (0.12 to 75.35 cm/s) suggests potential bimodal or outlier-contaminated distributions that may differentially affect paradigms."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "The dataset provides substantial trial counts for Combined and ICMS Only conditions but severely underrepresents Sham and Bright Visual Only conditions. Without paradigm-specific means and standard deviations, no definitive performance ranking can be established. The high overall success rate (~73%) and moderate path efficiency (~0.47) suggest mice generally perform well but with room for improvement. The Combined paradigm's dominance in the dataset likely reflects experimental design priorities, but this imbalance necessitates cautious interpretation of any comparative analyses. Angular dispersion values around 0.38 suggest moderately directed navigation strategies on average.",
  "limitations": [
    "No paradigm-specific descriptive statistics are provided—only global means and standard deviations across all paradigms combined.",
    "Extreme sample size imbalance (63.7% Combined vs. 4.3% Bright Visual Only) prevents reliable estimation of paradigm effects without appropriate weighting or resampling.",
    "Path Efficiency shows extreme right skew (max=29.82 vs. mean=0.47), indicating non-normal distributions that violate ANOVA assumptions.",
    "No information on mouse-level clustering or repeated-measures structure is incorporated in the available summaries.",
    "Temperature=0.0 and model=kimi with summary_only data view may limit exploration of interaction effects or complex patterns.",
    "Missing paradigm × performance variable cross-tabulations precludes identification of which paradigms improve or degrade specific metrics."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Compute paradigm-specific means, standard deviations, and confidence intervals for all five performance variables; apply appropriate mixed-effects models accounting for mouse-level clustering; conduct power analysis given the severe sample imbalance; and perform distribution diagnostics (especially for Path Efficiency and Time-to-Target) to determine whether transformation or robust methods are needed for valid inference."
}
